title: Perception Agents — Antje Barth, Amazon AGI Lab

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk centers on the perceive-plan-act agent loop and open-source harness components (annotation and verification tools) for perception agents. The perception agent harness is general-purpose infrastructure for builders, fitting both general_purpose and developer_platforms. The tools were recently open-sourced with an invitation for community contribution, indicating early-stage development. Assumes familiarity with agents and LLMs but does not require deep technical expertise. A conference presentation at the AI Engineer World's Fair. All evidence anchors are sourced directly from the transcript with grade 'said_in_transcript'.

summary: Antje Barth traces agent evolution: a year ago, finding and clicking a button was the hard problem; now agents drive browsers and desktop apps, but clicking was actually the easy part. The unsolved problem is end-to-end work across multiple systems—onboarding a new employee touches five systems, and while agents can perform each individual step, they fall apart at the seams between applications. This reveals a gap between capability and reliability. Without reliability there is no trust; if an agent deletes a database one in four times, nobody will use it again. Coding agents solved reliability first because code is verifiable—you can run, test, and check it. But knowledge work is messy: whether a report landed, whether a design is on brand—there are no unit tests for these. Humans handle messy work through shared context: two colleagues looking at the same screen solve problems quickly. Barth argues you don't need a bigger brain; you need shared context. Perception agents address this by completing a perceive-plan-act loop on screen, like robotics does in physical space. They read rendered screens (not scraped code), confirm their own output, work without APIs, and accept pointing-based input instead of long text descriptions. Amazon open-sourced two harness components: an annotation Chrome extension for marking screen elements with instructions, and a verification tool that checks agent output against design rules. Barth then demonstrates multimodal perception beyond screens: wearable transcription devices (B devices) listen during a design meeting, generate a transcript summary, and feed captured insights directly to the agent, which applies changes and triggers verification automatically. She emphasizes building in the open, invites the community to try the tools, give feedback, and mentions colleague Danielle Persik's podcast on human-agent interaction and Gaf Mishra's upcoming talk on RL to IRL. She closes with the goal of building AI that makes everyone smarter together.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Agents can perform individual workflow steps but fail at end-to-end work spanning multiple applications because real work lives in the seams between systems.
The industry solved capabilities (tool use, clicking, API calls) but has not solved reliability, which is prerequisite for trust.
Coding agents succeeded first because code is verifiable; most knowledge work has no equivalent of unit tests.
Humans solve messy work through shared context—looking at the same screen—rather than bigger brains.
Perception agents complete a perceive-plan-act loop on rendered screens, reading layout and state like humans do instead of scraping backend code.
Perception agents confirm their own output rather than firing actions and moving on, closing the reliability loop.
Amazon open-sourced annotation and verification tools for perception agents, enabling screen markup and automated design-rule checking.
Multimodal perception extends beyond screens: wearable devices can listen to discussions, transcribe meetings, and feed insights directly to the agent for action.
Amazon is building out the perception agent harness in the open, inviting community contributions and feedback to improve the patterns.
The ultimate goal is building AI that makes all of us smarter together, not individually.

sections.title: Introduction and the Evolution of Agent Capabilities
sections.summary: Barth welcomes the audience and reflects that a year ago clicking buttons was hard; now agents drive browsers and desktop apps, but clicking was the easy part. The actual work remains unsolved.

sections.title: The Problem: Real Work Lives in the Seams
sections.summary: Using employee onboarding as an example touching five systems, Barth explains that agents can do individual steps but fail end-to-end because real work lives in the seams between applications.

sections.title: The Capability-Reliability Gap
sections.summary: We taught computers to use computers—clicking, scrolling, typing, API calls—but capability alone isn't enough. Without reliability, trust cannot be built; a 60-80% success rate is insufficient when failures are catastrophic.

sections.title: Why Coding Agents Succeeded: Verification
sections.summary: Coding agents evolved from autocomplete to writing code and opening PRs. They achieved reliability because code is verifiable—you can run and test it. No one reads every generated line anymore.

sections.title: The Messiness of Knowledge Work
sections.summary: Most knowledge work is messy and has no unit tests. Whether a report landed or a design is on brand cannot be easily verified. This is where verification hits a wall.

sections.title: How Humans Collaborate: Shared Context
sections.summary: Humans handle messy work by collaborating—jumping on Zoom, looking at the same screen, pointing at systems. You don't need a bigger brain; you need shared context so the agent and human see the same thing.

sections.title: Introducing Perception Agents
sections.summary: Barth introduces perception agents that complete a perceive-plan-act loop on screen, like robotics. They read rendered screens in real time, react while you work, and understand what you mean by seeing what you see.

sections.title: Open Source Harness: Annotation and Verification
sections.summary: Amazon open-sourced two tools: an annotation Chrome extension for marking screen elements with instructions, and a verification tool that checks agent output against design rules through visual and user-flow checks, generating pass/fail reports.

sections.title: Beyond the Screen: Multimodal Perception with Wearable Devices
sections.summary: Barth demonstrates multimodal perception using B wearable transcription devices during a design meeting. The transcript is pulled into the agent interface; clicking apply sends design changes (yellow background, red heading, emoji change) to the agent, which applies them and triggers verification against design rules automatically. Design rule violations are flagged for human judgment.

sections.title: Call to Action: Building Together
sections.summary: Barth emphasizes building the harness in the open, invites the community to try the tools on GitHub, give feedback, and contribute. She recommends colleague Danielle Persik's podcast on human-agent interaction and Gaf Mishra's upcoming talk on RL to IRL. She closes with the goal of building AI that makes all of us smarter together.

demonstrations: Chrome extension annotation tool: user draws around a heading, marks it for color change to red, selects elements by hovering, requests font size doubling; agent captures location, style elements, and creates summary for implementation.

Verification tool: agent checks work against a design.md file containing design rules, performs visual checks (on-brand, layout) and user-flow checks (adding/deleting tasks like a real user), then writes a pass/fail report.

Multimodal perception demo: B wearable devices transcribe a design meeting; the transcript summary is pulled into the agent interface; clicking 'apply' sends insights (turn background yellow, heading red, change emoji) directly to the agent, which applies changes and triggers verification automatically against approved design rules.
limitations: Most knowledge work has no unit tests or verifiable answers.
Today's agents fire actions and move on without watching results or recovering from failures.
Current chatbot turn-taking rhythm causes long back-and-forth instead of real-time collaboration.
Most everyday software people use does not expose APIs.
quantitativeClaims: End-to-end agent workflows succeed maybe 60-80% of the time currently.
If an agent fails one in four times (e.g., deletes a database), users will never touch it again.
Reliability needs to be 'in the nines' to be trustworthy.
